en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Surāpānavagga 54.
The Training Rule on Disrespect.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Kosambī in Ghosita’s Monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Channa was practicing improper conduct.
The bhikkhus said to him:
"Friend Channa, do not do such a thing."
“This is not allowable.
Yet, out of disrespect, he continues to do it anyway.
Those monks who have few desires... [as before] ...they grumble, complain, and spread it about.
“How indeed could the Venerable Channa act with disrespect?
… [and so on] … “Is it true, Channa, that you act with disrespect?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“… How can you, foolish man, act with disrespect?
This, foolish man, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
“In case of disrespect, there is an offense of expiation.
Disrespect means:
There are two kinds of disrespect: disrespect for persons and disrespect for the Dhamma.

Disrespect for persons means that when one who is fully ordained is being addressed by someone established [in the discipline], if one shows disrespect thinking, "This person has been suspended, or is being ridiculed, or is being censured; his word shall not be heeded," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Disrespect toward the Dhamma" means:

when one who is fully ordained is being addressed by another who is fully ordained regarding what has been laid down [by the Buddha], thinking, "Lest this discourse be lost, destroyed, or disappear," yet out of a lack of desire to train, he shows disrespect; there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If the person addressed is fully ordained and he perceives them as such, yet he shows disrespect, there is an offense of expiation.
If one acts with disrespect toward one who is fully ordained while being in doubt [about their status], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one acts with disrespect toward one who is fully ordained while perceiving them as not fully ordained, there is an offense of expiation.
If one is addressed by means of what has not been prescribed—

If one shows disrespect, thinking, “This does not lead to effacement, nor to the purpose of the ascetic qualities, nor to inspiring confidence, nor to reduction [of defilements], nor to the arousal of energy,” there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one shows disrespect when being addressed by one who is not fully ordained— whether what was said was prescribed or not prescribed—

thinking, “This does not lead to effacement, nor to the purpose of the ascetic qualities, nor to inspiring confidence, nor to reduction, nor to the arousal of energy,” there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives someone who is not ordained as being ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one is uncertain regarding someone who is not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one perceives someone who is not ordained as being not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if he says, "Such is our teachers' instruction and inquiry," or if he is insane.
"For the first offender":
the fourth training rule concerning disrespect is concluded.
